---
layout: post
title: Is "AI slop" killing my game?
description: How often Steam reviews call a small indie game "AI slop", how many of those reviews are low effort, and how much they change the game's score.
---

"AI slop" is the insult of the moment for anything made with generative AI. On Steam, the common picture is a review bomb: waves of thumbs-down reviews that say "AI slop" and little else, dragging a game's score down. For an indie developer who used generative AI for some art, a voice-over, or a translation, that is a real thing to worry about.

To check how well that picture holds up, I looked at **95,899 Steam reviews across 799 paid indie games** launched in 2025 and 2026 that either disclose generative AI or have been flagged for it by Steam curators.

The short answer: **for almost all of these games, "AI slop" reviews are not killing the game.** They are rare, they are often more detailed than the stereotype suggests, and they barely move the overall score. Small games with fewer than 100 reviews are the main exception, where two or three negative reviews can knock a game down a Steam rating tier.

## Where the data comes from

The study starts from ten Steam curators that track generative-AI use. Filtering for indie games first launched on Steam on or after 1 January 2025 with between 10 and 2,000 Steam reviews produced 978 candidate games and 110,654 reviews (collected up to 16 November 2026, capped at the newest 1,000 reviews per game).

From there, I dropped 179 free-to-play titles, prologues, and demos (no money is at stake, nobody refunds them, and Steam mixes in non-purchase reviews), and dropped empty or link-only reviews. All prices use the regular store price rather than the snapshot sale price. That leaves **799 paid indie games** and **95,899 text reviews**.

A few things stand out about the pool before looking at AI at all:

- **Most of these games are small and well liked.** Six in ten have fewer than 50 reviews (median 34), and only 21 have more than 1,000. The median price is $6.20, and the median Steam score is 83% positive (59% sit at 80% or above, and 21% sit below 70%).
- **Most reviews are short, early, and not in English.** They span 30 languages, and only 39% are in English. The typical review is a sentence or two (median 35 tokens), written after 4.0 hours of play. Over a third (37%) arrive in launch week, and 59% in the first 30 days.
- **The curators fall into two very different camps.** Two large lists (*Game uses Ai* and *Games That Use AI Generation*) supply almost the whole pool, and like *AI Check* they mostly mirror Steam's own AI disclosure (93% to 95% of their games disclose AI). By contrast, *Does This Game Use GenAI?* investigates developers' Discord servers and social posts: only 24% of its games disclose AI on Steam, 40 of its 67 entries use "unsure" wording, and its picks are higher-rated (median 90%). That difference matters a lot when comparing disclosed and undisclosed games later.

> A curator flag is an accusation, not proof. Being in this dataset does not mean a game uses generative AI. Steam's *AI Generated Content Disclosure* is the developer's own statement, and even that is self-reported and unverified.

## Why keywords are not enough

A simple keyword search is the obvious way to count "AI slop" reviews, and I tested one as a baseline. Keywords have high precision (0.88 or better when they match), but they miss almost two-thirds of the real cases: recall is only 34% to 38%, which would have put the "AI slop" rate near 0.36% instead of 0.85%. Ordinary phrasing like "the voices are clearly AI" or "立绘是AI的" ("the character art is AI") slips past strict lists, while broad lists confuse "the enemy AI is dumb" or "the music fits the vibe" with generative AI.

Instead, every review containing any AI-like term across languages (6,555 of 95,899 reviews) was read in full in its original language by Claude Haiku and given one of three labels:

- **"AI slop"-type:** a derogatory verdict on generative-AI content ("AI slop", "lazy AI art", "soulless AI voices", "一眼AI", "нейрослоп", "vibe coded garbage").
- **Other generative-AI mention:** any other mention of generative AI in the game, whether complaining, neutral, or positive (including 201 reviews about in-game AI features like LLM-driven characters).
- **Not about generative AI:** everything else, including enemy/NPC AI, "slop" unrelated to AI, or AI as a story theme.

Reviews without any AI-like word were labelled "not" (a random audit of 2,275 of them found zero about generative AI). To see how consistent the model was, two independent passes over 740 reviews agreed on the main label 96% of the time, on what was called AI-made 97% to 100%, on attitude and "AI is the main reason" 93%, on effort 92% (labelled in its own dedicated pass), on personal insults 90%, and on how the reviewer knew 88%.

Here are eight real reviews from the dataset showing how the three labels separate in practice:

| Label | Thumb | Review |
|---|:-:|---|
| "AI slop"-type | 👎 | poor game all round, the AI art is lazy. |
| "AI slop"-type | 👎 | Been waiting for this one as it was in my calendar recommendations. Uninstalled and refunded after 7 minutes of tutorial. Could smell the AI all over. |
| "AI slop"-type | 👍 | its clunky, it uses AI slop, and its the same as all the other digging games out there....but theres penguins 10/10 game of the year |
| Other AI mention | 👎 | Played this way back, thought it was neat. Seems they're using generative AI for this. I can't support that. |
| Other AI mention | 👍 | Loving this game for the nonograms and the custom rulesets! Not a fan of the AI music, but I just have that muted for now. |
| Other AI mention (in-game) | 👍 | Lots of potential- keep updating the AI model and it will only get better |
| Not about gen AI | 👎 | I waited for this game for a year and all I got is disappointment. Ai is really bad and its more of a fun game than horror game. I dont recommend buying it rn |
| Not about gen AI | 👍 | The game runs smoothly on my PC and the whole atmosphere feels calm and relaxing. The music fits the vibe really well too. Good game! |

## How common are "AI slop" reviews?

Rare, even on a pool of games specifically flagged for AI.

Only **1 in 118 reviews (0.85%, or 815 reviews)** is "AI slop"-type, and **3.1%** mention generative AI in any way (2.9% leaving out the 201 reviews about in-game AI features). Because **85%** of "AI slop"-type reviews are thumbs-down, against 20% of all reviews, they make up **3.5%** (about **1 in 28**) of all negative reviews.

Reviews that mention generative AI *without* the insult look very different: they are thumbs-up more often than not (only 42% are negative). Read for their attitude to the AI itself, 56% are negative about it, 28% neutral, and 16% positive.

Narrowing down to the reviews that actually hurt a store page: only **0.72%** of all reviews (692) are "AI slop"-type with a thumbs-down, and just **0.04%** (39 reviews, about 1 in 2,459) add a refund on top.

They also pile up on a small slice of the catalogue. **71% of games (570 of 799) have no "AI slop"-type review at all**, and another 112 have exactly one. Meanwhile, the ten most called-out games hold **29%** of all "AI slop"-type reviews, and the top 20 hold **43%**. In 49 games (6%), at least 1 in 20 reviews is "AI slop"-type; in 13 games it is 1 in 10 or more. Even on the ten most called-out games, the label remains a minority view (1.6% to 6.5% of each game's reviews), and four of the ten still hold a Steam score of 80% or higher.

Per review, game size makes little difference: the "AI slop" rate sits between 0.6% and 1.4% across every size band (highest for games with 20 to 49 reviews), and the confidence intervals mostly overlap. Larger games are much more likely to have *at least one* such review (81% of games with 1,000 to 2,000 reviews vs. 7% of games with 10 to 19), simply because more reviews mean more chances.

## Are they really review bombers?

The stereotype is a drive-by refunder who posts "AI slop" during launch week and moves on. The data paints a different picture:

- **They mostly keep the game.** Only 39 of the 692 negative "AI slop" reviews (5.6%) come from a player Steam marks as refunded, compared with 4.4% of other thumbs-down reviews (odds ratio 1.30, Fisher *p* = 0.13).
- **They decide faster, and write more.** Half of negative "AI slop" reviewers played under 1.4 hours before reviewing, versus 2.8 hours for other unhappy players (59% wrote inside Steam's 2-hour refund window). Yet their median review is 279 characters, more than twice the length of other negative reviews. Their authors are also slightly more active reviewers overall (median 14 Steam reviews vs. 11).
- **Other players upvote them heavily.** Negative "AI slop" reviews are 3.5% of all negative reviews, but they collect **10% of all "helpful" votes** cast on negative reviews. Half have 5 or more helpful votes (other negative reviews: 23%). In 36 games (16% of those with any), an "AI slop"-type review sits as the single most-helpful review on the store page, making it far more visible to shoppers than its raw share suggests.
- **These gaps hold within the same game.** Across the 201 games that have both kinds of negative review, "AI slop" reviews have less playtime in 61% of games (*p* = 0.002), longer text in 72% (*p* < 10⁻⁹), and more helpful votes in 58% (*p* = 0.03).
- **They are not a launch-week raid, but the rate is climbing.** The "AI slop" rate is about the same in launch week as months later. Only 4% of games get one among their first 10 reviews (the ones that set a new game's initial Steam label); in games that do get one, the first is typically review number 28. Over calendar time, however, the rate has more than doubled: from **0.55%** of reviews in 2025 to **0.73%** in the first half of 2026, and **1.15%** since July 2026. Checking within the same 127 games reviewed before and after July 2026 confirms the rise (odds ratio 1.61, *p* = 3.1 × 10⁻⁵).

To test how much these reviews actually say, the model sorted both the 692 negative "AI slop"-type reviews and a random sample of 800 ordinary negative reviews from the same games into three tiers: **low effort** (a bare label, insult, or slogan with no reason given), **general reasons only** ("buggy", "boring", "soulless", "cash grab"), and **specific** (at least one concrete detail a reader can check, such as a named mechanic, bug, balance issue, or which asset looks off and why).

Low-effort one-liners are almost no more common among negative "AI slop" reviews than among ordinary negative reviews (**15%** vs. **14%**). Another **25%** give general reasons only (vs. **20%**), and the largest group by far is **specific** at **60%** (vs. **66%**; including thumbs-up "AI slop" reviews, 14% are low effort and 62% give specifics). Personal attacks on developers or other players are equally rare in both groups (**4%** vs. **4%**). Where the two groups do diverge is tone toward the game itself: **87%** of negative "AI slop" reviews are harsh about the game only (vs. **18%** of other negative reviews), largely because calling something "slop" already counts as harsh.

AI is also not always the sole reason for the thumbs-down. Across all "AI slop"-type reviews, AI is the main reason for the verdict in **57%** (62% of the thumbs-down ones, 28% of the thumbs-up ones). By depth, it is the main reason in **99%** of low-effort reviews and **79%** of general complaints, but only **39%** of specific reviews. Once a reviewer writes concrete details, AI is more often one gripe among several than the sole reason for the verdict.

When reviewers name what they think was AI-made, art and visuals dominate at 42%, while 39% name nothing specific and just call the game "AI slop" or "made with AI". And when reviewers explain how they know AI was used, most say they spotted it themselves rather than reading the store disclosure.

## How much do they change a game's Steam score?

To measure the direct score impact, I recomputed every game's positive review share after deleting every negative "AI slop"-type review. Across the whole dataset, the share of positive reviews moves from **79.6% to 80.2%** (a 0.6-point shift; deleting every negative review that mentions generative AI in *any* way moves it by 1.3 points).

- For **74% of games (593 of 799)**, nothing changes because they have no negative "AI slop" review.
- Among the 206 games that do, the typical difference is **1.5 points**.
- For **30 games (4%)**, the score shifts by **5 points or more** (the largest shift is 17 points), and **29 games** would carry a different Steam review label, most often *Mostly Positive* instead of *Mixed*.

Almost all of the big movers are tiny games: **28 of the 30 games with a 5+ point shift have fewer than 100 reviews** (median 20; the largest has 255). In a game with 20 reviews, every single review moves the score by 5 points, and Steam's labels have hard cut-offs at 40%, 70%, and 80%. No game with 500 or more reviews shifted by 5 points.

This calculation cuts both ways as a bound. On the direct score, it is an **upper bound**: deleting a review assumes the player would otherwise have stayed silent, even though many of these reviews also complain about bugs or gameplay and might have been thumbs-down anyway. On commercial impact, it is a **lower bound**: it cannot count shoppers who saw a heavily upvoted "AI slop" review on the store page and decided not to buy.

It is also worth checking whether games called "AI slop" more often are disliked for other reasons too. Among the 452 games with 30+ reviews, games where "AI slop" makes up 3% or more of reviews average about **70% positive** overall versus **82%** for games with none. Restricting to reviewers who *never mention AI in any way*, the gap still holds: **75% vs. 82%** (rank correlation −0.21, *p* = 5 × 10⁻⁶; holding other factors equal, each extra percentage point of "AI slop" reviews goes with an odds ratio of 0.94 for a positive review from non-AI reviewers, *p* = 0.0002). In practice, "AI slop" is often used as shorthand for a game that already feels rough or low-effort to players.

## Does disclosing AI hurt?

At first glance, disclosed games look worse: pooled across all 798 games with disclosure data, the median Steam score is 83% for disclosed games versus 88% for undisclosed ones. Split the dataset by where the games came from, however, and that gap disappears completely.

| Curator source | Discloses AI | Games | Median score | Mean score |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| All other curators | No | 52 | 81.5% | 79.8% |
| All other curators | Yes | 683 | 83.0% | 80.0% |
| Investigator (*Does This Game Use GenAI?*) | No | 49 | 90.0% | 83.1% |
| Investigator (*Does This Game Use GenAI?*) | Yes | 14 | 90.0% | 88.4% |

Within **both** groups, disclosed games score equal or slightly higher than undisclosed ones. The pooled 5-point gap is Simpson's paradox: almost half of the undisclosed games come from the investigator curator (*Does This Game Use GenAI?*), which researches higher-profile, better-reviewed games, while only 2% of disclosed games come from that list.

<li><i class="sw solid"></i>Discloses AI on Steam</li>
<li><i class="sw outline"></i>Doesn't disclose</li>
</ul>
<div class="rows">
<div class="row"><span class="cat">Pooled (all 798)</span><div class="bars"><div class="bar"><i class="solid" style="--v:0.8300"></i><b>83.0% (697)</b></div><div class="bar"><i class="outline" style="--v:0.8800"></i><b>88.0% (101)</b></div></div></div>
<div class="row"><span class="cat">Other curators</span><div class="bars"><div class="bar"><i class="solid" style="--v:0.8300"></i><b>83.0% (683)</b></div><div class="bar"><i class="outline" style="--v:0.8150"></i><b>81.5% (52)</b></div></div></div>

</div>
<p class="note">Full 0% to 100% scale; game counts in parentheses. Pooled, undisclosed games lead by 5 points, but within each curator group disclosed games tie or edge ahead.</p>
</figure>

Controlling for curator source, price, Early Access status, and time on sale in a Beta-Binomial model (which accounts for both game-to-game quality differences and review count), **disclosing AI on Steam has no detectable effect on a game's score**: **+0.4 percentage points** (95% range **−3.2 to +3.9 points**, odds ratio 1.02, *p* = 0.84). Dropping the investigator curator altogether gives **−0.2 points** (*p* = 0.93), and alternative weighting schemes agree. Because there are only 52 undisclosed games outside the investigator curator, the data rules out a large score collapse from disclosing AI, though it cannot rule out a modest 3- to 4-point difference either way. One side finding from the same model: higher-priced games receive a lower share of positive reviews (odds ratio 0.88 per log-unit of price, *p* = 0.003), which fits players being harsher when more money is on the line.

Disclosing *does* go with getting the label itself, however. Disclosed games account for 780 of the 815 "AI slop"-type reviews and receive them at **4.2× the rate** of undisclosed ones (0.97% vs. 0.23%; adjusted game-level odds ratio 3.0, 95% range 1.51 to 5.87, *p* = 0.002). Two explanations fit, and this data cannot separate them: the disclosure may point reviewers toward the AI, or disclosed games may simply use more (or more visible) AI than games that are only accused, some of which may use none at all. On disclosed games, only 5% of "AI slop" reviewers cite the disclosure while 59% say they noticed the AI themselves, though someone who read the disclosure first may still describe what they noticed.

What the AI was used for matters just as much. Sorting all 697 developer disclosure texts with Claude Haiku (99% to 100% agreement across two passes, avoiding keyword errors on negations like "no AI voices or music"), games that use AI in something players see or hear get the label at **2.4× the rate** of games that use it only for text, translation, or code (1.04% vs. 0.43%; adjusted odds ratio 2.4, *p* = 0.002). By individual use, the rate is highest for voice (1.5% across 61 games) and music and sound (1.2% across 141 games), while art and visuals is by far the most common use (524 games, 1.04%).

## Language and culture matter too

The "AI slop" label is not used evenly across Steam's audience. English reviewers use it most often (1.31% of reviews, with 4.48% mentioning generative AI at all), followed closely by Russian (1.07%). Simplified Chinese, the second-largest language in the dataset at 23,800 reviews, sits at 0.58%. German, Turkish, Korean, and Japanese reviews rarely use the label (0.21% to 0.42%), even though Korean and Japanese reviewers still mention generative AI in neutral or other ways at 1.7% to 1.9%.

The tone of the phrase itself varies by language. In the keyword check, English "AI slop" is the harshest: 85% of reviews using it are negative. Russian sits in between at 67%. Chinese *AI味* is much softer at 51%, reading closer to "has an AI feel" than a flat verdict.

## A case in point: *Slotbound*

If you have been following AI game dev circles recently, you have probably seen ***Slotbound*** (Optima Arch) making the rounds as the [poster child for AI game dev ("vibe-coded") success](https://www.reddit.com/r/aigamedev/comments/1y51so0/a_solo_developer_just_vibecoded_his_first_game/): a $9.99 roguelike auto-battler with tower defence, built by a solo developer, launched on 13 November 2026, and openly disclosing generative AI for visual assets and promotional materials on its Steam store page.

It happens to sit right inside this dataset, though the main study's 16 November snapshot caught only its launch weekend (605 reviews). Nine days later, on 25 November 2026, *Slotbound* had taken off past the study's 2,000-review cap to **2,405 reviews** on Steam (**2,400 clean text reviews** after dropping 5 empty or link-only ones). Running the exact same pipeline on *Slotbound*'s full, uncapped history (two independent Claude Haiku passes over all 43 reviews with an AI-like word: 98% agreement, plus 100% agreement with the main study on the 600 overlapping reviews still on Steam, an audit of 300 non-AI-word reviews that found zero AI mentions, and a 400-review baseline of ordinary thumbs-down reviews) lets us check what Steam buyers actually said once the game broke out:

- **AI mentions stayed rare, and mostly positive.** Only **28 of 2,400 reviews (1.17%, 95% range 0.81% to 1.68%)** mention generative AI at all, well below the 799-game pool (3.07%) and its largest 1,000 to 2,000 review games (2.67%). Only **4 reviews (0.17%, range 0.06% to 0.43%)** are "AI slop"-type (3 if counting only reviews where both passes agree). Even though the disclosure names only art and promotional materials, 5 reviews say the code is AI-written too and several call the whole game AI-made, yet **21 of the 28 AI mentions are thumbs-up**: players who know the game uses AI and recommend it anyway.
- **The few negative AI reviews look like the rest of the negative reviews.** Out of **449 thumbs-down reviews**, only **7 (1.6%)** mention generative AI and **3 (0.7%)** are "AI slop"-type. On effort, those 7 break down as **1 low effort**, **3 general**, and **3 specific** (with 1 personal attack; AI is the main reason in 4 of the 7). Across *Slotbound*'s 400 sampled ordinary thumbs-down reviews, the split is **14% low effort**, **28% general**, and **58% specific** (with 6% personal attacks). Notably, the 3 negative "AI slop"-type reviews were written after **9.1**, **30.3**, and **46.8 hours** of play, focused on replayability, RNG, and late-game balance rather than drive-by one-liners.
- **The score barely moved.** Across all 2,400 reviews, *Slotbound* holds **81.3% positive** (*Very Positive*). Deleting its 3 negative "AI slop"-type reviews moves the score to **81.4%** (**+0.1 points**); deleting all 7 negative AI mentions moves it to **81.5%** (**+0.2 points**). Its Steam label stays *Very Positive* in every scenario: it would take **39 more thumbs-down reviews** with no new thumbs-up (nearly 6 times its total negative AI mentions) to pull it down to *Mostly Positive*.

A single game picked after the fact because it is selling well does not show how often AI-assisted games succeed. What *Slotbound* does show is that openly disclosing generative AI in visual assets, even on a game players widely describe as AI-made, does not stop a game from having a strong launch when the core loop clicks.

---

## Limitations

- **Curator sample only:** Every game here was flagged by at least one AI-tracking curator. That is not every game on Steam or every game that uses AI, and there is no control group of unflagged games to compare against.
- **Buyer selection:** Steam reviews come only from people who bought the game. Players who saw the AI disclosure (or suspected heavy AI use) and skipped the game do not appear in this data.
- **No measure of how much AI:** A game with a few generated icons counts the same as one built heavily with generative AI, and some curator-accused games may use none at all.
- **Small-model labelling:** Reviews and disclosures were labelled by Claude Haiku, Anthropic's least capable model at the time of writing. Some labels will be wrong, even where two independent passes agree 88% to 96% of the time.
- **No sarcasm tag:** Joking uses of "AI slop" are counted alongside serious ones, which is why the score analysis focuses on thumbs-down reviews.

*Data was collected up to 16 November 2026 and is not released publicly. The analysis code and notebook (`aislop_analysis.ipynb`) were written with Claude; the direction of the analysis was set by me.*
